questions.stem: What does the first ionisation energy remove?

options.text: A mole of electrons leaving a mole of gaseous atoms, which become gaseous 1+ ions
options.explanation: The full definition names the amounts and the gaseous states.

options.text: One electron from the nucleus
options.explanation: Electrons are removed from orbitals, never the nucleus.

options.text: One mole of electrons from solid atoms
options.explanation: The definition requires the gaseous state.

options.text: Two moles of electrons per mole of atoms
options.explanation: IE1 removes exactly one electron per atom.

questions.stem: Why are all ionisation energies endothermic?

options.text: Because ions are heavier than atoms
options.explanation: Removing electrons makes ions lighter.

options.text: Energy must be supplied to pull electrons away from the nucleus's attraction
options.explanation: Separation against attraction always absorbs energy.

options.text: Because electrons release energy when leaving
options.explanation: Leaving costs energy; falling in releases it.

options.text: Because the process happens at high temperature
options.explanation: The measurement conditions do not fix the sign.

questions.stem: Calcium's IE2 is defined by which equation?

options.explanation: That is the third.

options.text: Ca (s) -> Ca+ (aq) + e-
options.explanation: Wrong state on both counts.
The second electron leaves the gaseous 1+ ion.

options.text: Ca (g) -> Ca+ (g) + e-
options.explanation: That is the first ionisation energy.

questions.stem: Why is calcium's IE3 (+4912) far larger than its IE2 (+1145)?

options.text: Because calcium's nucleus gains a proton
options.explanation: The nucleus is unchanged during ionisation.

options.text: Because the ion becomes gaseous
options.explanation: It was gaseous already.

options.text: Because electrons repel the incoming energy
options.explanation: Repulsion plays no such role.

options.text: The third electron comes from a principal shell closer to the nucleus (3p vs 4s)
options.explanation: The shell drop raises the attraction sharply.

questions.stem: Under which standard conditions are ionisation energies measured?

options.text: 298 K and 101 kPa, on gaseous atoms
options.explanation: The definition pins temperature and pressure.

options.text: 0 degrees C and 1 atmosphere
options.explanation: Those are s.t.p. conditions, not the IE standard.

options.text: 293 K and 101.3 kPa
options.explanation: That is r.t.p., used for gas volumes.

options.text: Whatever temperature the experiment uses
options.explanation: The standard set is part of the definition.

questions.modelAnswer: It is the energy that strips a mole of electrons from a mole of gaseous 1+ ions, converting those ions into gaseous 2+ ions.

questions.stem: State calcium's first, second and third ionisation energies.
questions.modelAnswer: IE1 = +590 kJ mol^-1, IE2 = +1145 kJ mol^-1 and IE3 = +4912 kJ mol^-1, all endothermic.

questions.stem: Explain why the ionisation energy sequence for one element always rises.
questions.modelAnswer: Each removal leaves fewer electrons shielding a same-sized nucleus and increases the ion's positive charge, so the remaining electrons feel a stronger pull; the energy bill therefore climbs with every electron removed, with jumps at shell boundaries.

questions.stem: Write the equation, with state symbols, for calcium's first ionisation energy and quote its value.
questions.modelAnswer: Ca (g) -> Ca+ (g) + e- , IE1 = +590 kJ mol^-1; the gaseous states are part of the definition.

questions.stem: How many orbitals does a p sub-shell contain, and what total does that permit?

options.text: Three orbitals holding three
options.explanation: Each orbital holds TWO electrons.

options.text: Three orbitals, holding six electrons in total
options.explanation: Each orbital takes two electrons of opposite spin: 3 x 2 = 6.

options.text: One orbital holding two electrons
options.explanation: That describes an s sub-shell.

options.text: Five orbitals holding ten
options.explanation: That describes a d sub-shell.

questions.stem: Increasing nuclear charge across a period has what effect on first ionisation energy?

options.text: It has no effect until a shell fills
options.explanation: The effect is continuous across the period.

options.text: It first raises then lowers IE
options.explanation: The general trend rises across a period.

options.text: It raises IE, because more protons attract the outer electrons more strongly
options.explanation: The pull grows with the proton count.

options.text: It lowers IE, because atoms get heavier
options.explanation: Mass does not set the pull.

questions.stem: Why does increased shielding make the outer electron easier to remove?

options.text: Because shielding adds protons
options.explanation: Shielding adds no protons.

options.text: Because the outer electron pairs up
options.explanation: Pairing is a separate factor.

options.text: Because shields reduce distance
options.explanation: Shielding acts between distance and charge.

options.text: Inner-shell electrons screen the outer electron from the nucleus's full attraction
options.explanation: The net pull the outer electron feels is reduced.

questions.stem: What is spin-pair repulsion and what does it cause?

options.text: Two electrons sharing an orbital repel slightly, so paired electrons are removed more easily
options.explanation: The pairing offsets nuclear attraction.

options.text: Opposite spins attract, stabilising pairs
options.explanation: Repulsion, not attraction, characterises the pair.

options.text: It only affects noble gases
options.explanation: It operates wherever electrons pair.

options.text: It raises ionisation energy for pairs
options.explanation: It LOWERS the energy needed.

questions.stem: Why do noble gases show very high ionisation energies while group 1 metals show low ones?

options.text: Because noble gases carry charge
options.explanation: They are neutral atoms.

options.text: Noble gases hold full sub-shells with strong, unshielded nuclear pull on outer electrons; group 1 metals have a single, shielded, easily lost electron
options.explanation: Configuration decides the bill.

options.text: Because noble gases are heavier
options.explanation: Mass is not the driver.

options.text: Because group 1 metals are gases
options.explanation: They are metals.

questions.stem: State the orbital count and electron capacity of s, p and d sub-shells.
questions.modelAnswer: s holds one orbital (2 electrons), p holds three orbitals (6 electrons) and d holds five orbitals (10 electrons).

questions.stem: State the four factors affecting the size of a first ionisation energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear charge, distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus, shielding by inner electrons, and spin-pair repulsion.

questions.stem: Explain why attraction falls off rapidly with distance and why that matters for large atoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrostatic attraction weakens steeply as separation grows, so an outer electron two shells further out feels dramatically less pull; that is why large atoms with many inner shells lose their outer electrons at low energies compared with compact atoms of the same group.

questions.stem: Predict, with reasons, which loses an electron more easily: a lithium 2s electron or a helium 1s electron.
questions.modelAnswer: Lithium's 2s electron: it sits farther from the nucleus and is shielded by the 1s pair, so it is removed far more easily than helium's unshielded, close-in 1s electron.
